planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Meadowlark was bred jointly by South Dakota State University and the USDA specifically for flower-bud hardiness in harsh northern Plains winters.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom. Meadowlark was bred for exceptional cold hardiness, its flower buds surviving winter temperatures that kill the buds of most other forsythia cultivars outright, so it reliably produces its bright golden-yellow late-winter flower display even after the harshest northern winters where other forsythias bloom sparsely or not at all. The vigorous, upright, arching shrub grows quickly into a large specimen or informal hedge and tolerates a wide range of soils once established. Prune right after flowering to shape or control size, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's flowers.

common_name: Minnesota Snowflake Mock Orange (Cold-Hardy Double-Flowered Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Minnesota Snowflake was bred at the University of Minnesota specifically for reliable cold hardiness and heavy double bloom.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Minnesota Snowflake was bred at the University of Minnesota for gardeners in harsh northern climates who wanted the classic mock orange fragrance without losing flower buds to winter cold, and it remains one of the most reliably cold-hardy double-flowered mock orange cultivars available. Its pure white, fully double flowers open in dense clusters along arching branches in late spring, carrying the same sweet, orange-blossom scent that gives the species its common name. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's display; established plants tolerate a wide range of soils and need little routine care.
